cards.q: What is centripetal force?
cards.c: A centre-seeking force needed for any curved path, acting along the radius towards the centre.
w: A centrifugal force pushing the object outward
A linear force acting forward along the flight path
A gravitational force pulling the aircraft downward

cards.q: For an aircraft in a turn, what is the centripetal force also called?
cards.c: The horizontal component of lift.
w: The vertical component of weight
The total engine thrust vector
The induced drag component

cards.q: What does the third law of motion say about centripetal force, according to the source?
cards.c: It is opposed by an equal and opposite force called the centrifugal force (a centre-fleeing force).
w: It creates an infinite acceleration toward the center
It eliminates all aerodynamic drag on the airframe
It converts gravitational energy directly into kinetic energy

cards.q: What happens to an object on a string if the string is released? Which law explains it?
cards.c: The object flies off in a straight line at a tangent; explained by Newton's first law of motion.
w: The object flies straight outward along the radius; explained by Newton's second law
The object stops instantly; explained by Newton's third law
The object spirals downward; explained by gravity

cards.q: Does the released object fly outwards along the radius? Explain.
cards.c: No, the object goes off straight along the tangent (touching the circle at one point), not radially outwards.
w: Yes, centrifugal force throws it straight out along the radius
Yes, because the string's tension pushes it outward upon release
No, it falls straight down to the center of the earth

cards.q: Can any object, car or aircraft, turn without centripetal force?
cards.c: No, without centripetal force, no object can be made to turn.
w: Yes, cars can turn using engine power alone without any sideways force
Yes, aircraft turn purely through gravity without centripetal force
Yes, momentum automatically curves any path without forces

cards.q: On what three things does centripetal force depend, and how?
cards.c: Directly proportional to the mass (or weight) of the body, directly proportional to the square of its speed, and inversely proportional to the radius of the turn.
w: Directly to speed, inversely to mass, and independent of radius
Directly to radius and mass, inversely to speed cubed
Independent of mass, directly to radius squared

cards.q: Write the centripetal-force formula in lb and in newtons.
cards.c: Centripetal force = (W * V^2) / (g * r) in lb, or (m * v^2) / r in newtons.
w: Centripetal force = (W * r) / V^2 in lb
Centripetal force = (m * g * r) / V in newtons
Centripetal force = W * V * r in lb

cards.q: What does each symbol W, V^2, r, g mean? Give both unit systems for g.
cards.c: W = weight (or m = mass); V^2 = square of TAS; r = radius of turn; g = gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s^2 or 32.2 ft/s^2).
w: W = wind speed; V^2 = volume squared; r = rate; g = gear ratio
W = wing loading; V^2 = velocity; r = roll rate; g = gravity constant (10 m/s^2)
W = watts; V^2 = voltage; r = resistance; g = ground speed

cards.q: Give the formula for acceleration towards the centre.
cards.c: Acceleration = V^2 / r.
w: Acceleration = r / V^2
Acceleration = g * r * V
Acceleration = V / (g * r)

cards.q: Find the centripetal force for W = 3220 lb, V = 100 ft/s, r = 1000 ft, g = 32.2 ft/s^2.
w: F = 100 lb

cards.q: Find the centripetal force in newtons for m = 1000 kg, V = 50 m/s, r = 300 m.
w: F = 50,000 newtons
F = 15,000 newtons

cards.q: What happens to the centripetal force if the speed is doubled and the radius is unchanged?
cards.c: It increases by a factor of four (doubling speed needs four times the force because speed is squared).
w: It doubles because force is directly proportional to speed
It remains completely unchanged
It halves because speed and force are inversely related

cards.q: Find the acceleration towards the centre if V = 60 m/s and r = 360 m.
w: Acceleration = 60 / 360 = 0.16 m/s^2
Acceleration = 360 / 60 = 6 m/s^2
Acceleration = 60 * 360 = 21,600 m/s^2

cards.q: How is the centripetal force of an aircraft derived?
cards.c: By resolving the inclined total lift force into a vertical lift component and a horizontal lift component.
w: By increasing engine thrust to push the aircraft sideways
By deflecting the rudder to push tail air outward
By shifting fuel weight from wing to wing

cards.q: In Figure 2.22, name the three arrows (other than weight) and how they are related.
cards.c: Total lift, vertical lift component, and centripetal force (horizontal lift component); total lift is the vector sum of the two components.
w: Thrust, drag, and lift; they sum to zero
Lift, side force, and centrifugal force; they balance weight
Centripetal force, centrifugal force, and gravity; they form a closed loop

cards.q: What is the "double role" of lift in a turn?
cards.c: It must provide the horizontal component to create centripetal force and a vertical component large enough to maintain constant height.
w: It must accelerate the aircraft forward while simultaneously slowing it down
It must generate cabin pressurization and control surface response
It must balance both weight and engine torque simultaneously

cards.q: Why does the aircraft tend to descend if the angle of attack is not increased in a turn?
cards.c: Because tilting the total lift vector sideways reduces the vertical lift component below the aircraft's weight.
w: Because banking increases aircraft weight instantly
Because turning turns off the engine automatically
Because horizontal lift pulls the aircraft downward toward the earth

cards.q: What must the pilot do to the angle of attack in a level turn, and what is the consequence for drag and power?
cards.c: The pilot must increase the angle of attack; this causes a surge in induced drag, which requires more engine power to keep speed constant.
w: The pilot must decrease the angle of attack; drag drops and speed increases
The pilot must keep angle of attack constant; power remains unchanged
The pilot must shut down the engine to prevent overspeeding

cards.q: What is a steep turn?
cards.c: A turn having an angle of bank in excess of 45 degrees.
w: Any turn executed above 10,000 feet altitude
A turn where the aircraft banks vertically at 90 degrees
A turn performed with the engine at idle power

cards.q: Why do larger bank angles need a larger angle of attack?
cards.c: Because steeper banks tilt more lift sideways, requiring a larger total-lift increment (higher angle of attack) to keep the vertical lift equal to weight.
w: Because higher bank angles make the wings heavier
Because speed automatically drops to zero in a steep bank
Because gravity pulls the tail down during a bank

cards.q: What happens as the aircraft in a steep turn reaches a very low speed?
cards.c: The angle of attack and induced drag become so high that full power is usually necessary, risking an acceleration stall.
w: The aircraft magically gains altitude without power
The wings fold automatically due to excess G-force
The flight controls lock completely

cards.q: What does Figure 2.23 show about the lift required in a steep turn compared with Figure 2.22?
cards.c: A much longer, more tilted total-lift arrow is shown to account for the steeper bank angle.
w: A shorter, flatter lift vector because less lift is needed at high bank angles
No change in lift magnitude, only a change in engine thrust
An inverted lift vector pointing toward the ground

cards.q: Define wing loading, what does it affect?
cards.c: Wing loading is the weight of the aircraft divided by the wing area; it affects both the maximum and minimum stalling speeds.
w: Wing loading is wing area divided by weight; it affects only engine fuel consumption
Wing loading is total lift minus drag; it affects only cruise altitude
Wing loading is engine power divided by mass; it affects climb rate only

cards.q: What is the modern tendency regarding wing loading and landing speeds?
cards.c: Higher wing loading (smaller area, higher speed), using movable flaps to cut landing speeds.
w: Lower wing loading (larger area, lower speed) with no flaps allowed
Constant wing loading across all aircraft types regardless of size
Removing wings entirely in favor of jet thrust

cards.q: What is load factor n, and what is its value in straight and level flight?
cards.c: Load factor is lift divided by weight (n = L/W); its value is 1 in straight and level flight[span_0](start_span)[span_0](end_span).
w: Load factor is thrust divided by drag; its value is 0
Load factor is weight divided by wing area; its value equals wing loading
Load factor is centripetal force multiplied by gravity; its value is 2

cards.q: How is load factor related to bank angle according to the source?
cards.c: It varies as the secant of the bank angle (n = sec phi = 1 / cos phi)[span_1](start_span)[span_1](end_span).
w: It varies as the tangent of the bank angle
It varies as the sine of the bank angle squared
It remains constant regardless of bank angle

cards.q: What is the load factor in a 60 degree bank turn?
cards.c: n = 1 / cos(60 deg) = 1 / 0.5 = 2.0 (the aircraft experiences 2 g)[span_2](start_span)[span_2](end_span).
w: n = 1.0 (no change from level flight)
n = 1.414 (equal to square root of two)
n = 4.0 (quadruples due to secant scaling)

cards.q: How is the stalling speed in a maneuver related to the load factor?
cards.c: New stalling speed equals basic stalling speed multiplied by the square root of the load factor (V_new = V_s * sqrt(n))[span_3](start_span)[span_3](end_span).
w: New stalling speed equals basic stalling speed multiplied by n cubed
New stalling speed equals basic stalling speed divided by n
Stalling speed is completely independent of load factor

cards.q: If a basic stalling speed is 85 knots, what is the stalling speed in a 60 degree bank turn (n = 2)?
cards.c: V_new = 85 * sqrt(2) approx 120 knots[span_4](start_span)[span_4](end_span).
w: V_new = 85 * 2 = 170 knots
V_new = 85 knots (unchanged)
V_new = 85 / 1.414 = 60 knots

cards.q: What is an accelerated (high-speed) stall in a turn, and what causes it?
cards.c: An accelerated stall happens when a high bank angle forces the plane to reach the critical angle of attack at a higher speed due to increased load factor[span_5](start_span)[span_5](end_span).
w: An accelerated stall happens when the engine runs out of fuel at high altitudes
An accelerated stall is caused by flying below the minimum design speed in straight flight
An accelerated stall occurs when landing flaps are deployed at supersonic speeds

cards.q: What can happen if one wing stalls before the other during an accelerated stall?
cards.c: The aircraft may experience a sudden roll toward the unlifted wing, known as a flicking movement due to unequal lift distribution[span_6](start_span)[span_6](end_span).
w: The aircraft immediately pitches straight up into a vertical climb
The flight controls lock completely in place
The engine shuts down automatically to prevent structural failure

cards.q: How is recovery initiated from an accelerated stall?
cards.c: By moving the control column forward, decreasing the angle of attack, and thereby unstalling the aircraft[span_7](start_span)[span_7](end_span).
w: By pulling back harder on the stick to regain altitude immediately
By applying full rudder in the direction of the spin
By shutting down all electrical systems

cards.q: What does a wing always stall at, and why is an accelerated stall called "high-speed"?
cards.c: A wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack, but at a higher speed in a turn because increased G-force raises the stall speed[span_8](start_span)[span_8](end_span).
w: It stalls at a higher angle of attack only when flying above 300 knots
It is called high-speed because the engine is pushed to maximum RPM
It is called high-speed because air density drops rapidly

cards.q: What practical factors limit the minimum radius of a turn?
cards.c: Maximum permitted load factor (G-limit), maximum lift before reaching the stall, airspeed, and available engine performance.
w: The amount of fuel remaining in the wing tanks only
The length of the runway used for takeoff
The color scheme and paint weight of the aircraft airframe

cards.q: If an aircraft reaches its maximum permitted G-load, can it keep increasing its turning force indefinitely?
cards.c: B. No (turning force is restricted by structural G-limits and stall boundaries).
w: A. Yes, G-limits can be exceeded safely without structural damage
A. Yes, engine thrust compensates for all structural load limits
B. No, because gravity turns off during high-G maneuvers

cards.q: What determines maximum rate of turn?
cards.c: Airspeed, how much turning force the aircraft can produce, and balancing turning performance against stall and structural limits.
w: The total weight of the pilot and baggage capacity
The number of engines mounted on the fuselage
The geographical latitude of the flight path

cards.q: What is corner speed in aircraft performance?
cards.c: Corner speed is approximately the speed at which the aircraft can reach its maximum permitted load factor without exceeding its stall limit (maximum turning performance without stalling).
w: Corner speed is the maximum safe speed for lowering landing gear
Corner speed is the speed where induced drag drops completely to zero
Corner speed is the minimum speed required to start the engine

cards.q: What governs the minimum radius of a turn according to the equations in the text?
cards.c: The minimum radius is set by speed squared and the maximum lift coefficient (r = (V^2 / g) * (C_Lmax / C_L)), with engine power as the final deciding factor[span_9](start_span)[span_9](end_span)[span_10](start_span)[span_10](end_span).
w: The minimum radius is determined entirely by aircraft weight and fuel capacity
The minimum radius depends strictly on propeller pitch and rudder deflection
The minimum radius is fixed at 500 feet for all aircraft types

cards.q: What is the difference between a minimum radius turn and a maximum rate turn?
cards.c: A minimum radius turn gives the smallest physical circle, while a maximum rate turn gives the shortest time to change heading (highest angular velocity)[span_11](start_span)[span_11](end_span)[span_12](start_span)[span_12](end_span).
w: A minimum radius turn uses zero engine power, while maximum rate uses full power
A minimum radius turn is performed upside down, while maximum rate is level
There is no difference between the two terms in aerodynamics

cards.q: What three conditions provide a maximum-rate turn?
cards.c: Fly at the stalling speed, fly at the maximum load factor, and fly in air that is as dense as possible[span_13](start_span)[span_13](end_span).
w: Fly at maximum speed, minimum load factor, and at maximum service ceiling altitude
Fly with full flaps, zero engine power, and a 90-degree bank angle
Fly straight and level without banking while accelerating rapidly

cards.q: Why does a climbing turn tend towards an over-bank, and what must the pilot do?
cards.c: The outer wing travels a greater distance and moves faster, generating more lift and increasing the bank angle; the pilot must hold bank off using opposite aileron[span_14](start_span)[span_14](end_span)[span_15](start_span)[span_15](end_span).
w: The inner wing generates more lift because it moves slower, pulling the nose down; the pilot must pull back harder
The tailplane stalls from excess downwash, forcing a level recovery
Gravity pulls the heavy side down, requiring full rudder application

cards.q: What is the effect on the outer wing vs inner wing in a descending turn?
cards.c: In a descending turn the inner wing has the greater angle of attack, and the bank must be held on by the pilot[span_16](start_span)[span_16](end_span).
w: The outer wing completely loses all lift instantly
Both wings experience zero angle of attack due to downward momentum
The aircraft enters an immediate unrecoverable spin toward the outer wing

cards.q: What is a pull-out maneuver, and what sequence of events occurs when a pilot pulls back on the control column during a descent?
cards.c: When the pilot pulls back, the elevator deflects upward, raising the nose, increasing the wing's angle of attack and lift, which curves the flight path upward to transition the aircraft from descending to level flight.
w: When the pilot pulls back, the spoilers deploy, the nose drops, and the aircraft dives steeper
When the pilot pulls back, engine thrust cuts off, airspeed drops, and the aircraft enters a flat spin
When the pilot pulls back, the flaps retract automatically, causing a sudden loss of altitude
